text: Engineering accreditation (Washington Accord) defines seven attributes of a Complex Engineering Problem. Tap each one to see what it means and how we help.

items.title: Depth of knowledge required
items.text: Solving the problem needs in-depth engineering knowledge — fundamentals plus specialist, research-based understanding — rather than routine application of standard methods.
items.example: Designing a low-cost water-quality monitor needs sensing, signal processing, power and data-communication knowledge together.

items.title: Range of conflicting requirements
items.text: Technical, engineering and other issues pull in different directions — cost versus performance, speed versus safety — and must be balanced.
items.example: A rural health-record app must be secure, work offline, stay cheap and be simple for first-time users.

items.title: Depth of analysis required
items.text: There are no obvious solutions. Abstract thinking, originality and first-principles analysis are needed to build suitable models.
items.example: Predicting traffic flow across a city needs custom models, not a textbook formula.

items.title: Familiarity of issues
items.text: The problem involves infrequently encountered issues, so familiar patterns and past solutions do not simply transfer.
items.example: Adapting a known IoT design to extreme flood conditions raises issues the standard design never faced.

items.title: Extent of applicable codes
items.text: The problem lies outside what standards and codes of practice explicitly cover, so judgement is needed where the rules run out.
items.example: Deploying a new energy-storage method where no safety standard exists yet.

items.title: Extent of stakeholder involvement
items.text: Many groups with widely differing needs are involved — users, regulators, communities, funders — and their needs must be reconciled.
items.example: A new riverside market affects traders, residents, city authorities and the environment.

items.title: Interdependence
items.text: The problem is made of many parts or sub-problems that depend on each other, so a change in one ripples through the rest.
items.example: A smart-grid project where generation, storage, billing and user apps constantly influence each other.
